title: What 500+ Production Environments Taught Us About Shipping AI Agents

segments.text: Good morning. Nice to meet you all. I'm Liran. I'm the VP of AI at Coralogix. And today we are going I'm going to share with you our experience with
building an agent that is production facing today serving actually over 1,000 customers in production environment. And over this journey, we've had some interesting learning
experiences I'm going to share with you. So, let's start with what is Ollie. Ollie's our agentic AI which we serve for our customers. Maybe a step
backward. Coralogix is an observability platform. So, you send logs, metrics, traces every production telemetry that you have to Coralogix. And then you can build
dashboards, monitor, track them, get alerts, identify what is the root cause and so on and so forth. Having all these data is huge has the huge potential
to actually get a lot of insights with AI. So, when we started, so this is kind of how we started Ollie. You see Ollie on the
screen. The when what Ollie is doing, Ollie's an agentic system. It's not just one agent behind the scenes. There are multiple sub agents collaborating
together on top of the knowledge that we've built. Um and what you see here is actually an example of a user coming in and instead
of manually investigating a production issue, just sharing, "Hey, users complain on slowness in Europe. Can you help me out understand what's going on?" And Ollie would go behind the scenes and
query logs, query metrics, create correlation with traces, identify hopefully what is the root cause or for the very least help you and shortcut the
way to finding the root cause. So, how how we actually started with Ollie. This was January 2025. Beforehand I was the CEO of Aporia where
we've done observe AI observability platform and we got acquired by Coralogix. So, we just got acquired. Our first 2 weeks at Coralogix at the
company, um and I remember we have this brilliant vision of what an observability agent could do. Now, I know today it may sound obvious,
yeah, like it's clear that what agents can do. But yes, 1 and 1/2 years ago, it sounded like, "Wow, that could be amazing if we would have agent that
would do that, right?" Um So, we built a quite an impressive demo. Um honestly, it took us 2 weeks of Ollie which was capable that in the
demo you could have seen um logs, metrics traces investigation integration with code base in in GitHub repos, um investigation of all of that and getting
to the root cause. And still, even though we had that on January 2025, as you can see, we started internal beta at the our company only on July.
So, 6 month. And then the month after, August, we started with design partners, real customers who work with us, who see us technical um partners.
And I think this is where things started to get interesting. So, until that part, everything was going extremely well, you know, it Ollie was very very impressive.
Obviously, the demo was kind of shook everyone. Um and after we rolled out to our design partners, we had a couple of design partners we worked with.
We wanted to upgrade the model version, right? So, for example, we updated from Sonnet 4.5 to 4.6. What would you expect to happen? Right?
To improve. The model should be better, right? On all benchmarks we uh and and so on is is better. So, what? Like if we upgrade the model,
Ollie should now be better. So, the funny thing is um the model got better, but our agent actually got worse. So, we started actually getting complaints from our
desired smart partners saying, "Hey guys, like what's going on? Uh I I feel like Ollie is not the same Ollie that we had last week.
Um what have you changed? I I feel like Ollie is not providing the exact answers like it used to." Um so, it was very very interesting for
us. And what we realized is upgrading a model completely changes the behavior of your agent. Okay, so you cannot just do it. It's not just
updating one single string. Um so, for that what we have realized we need to do is for every model change, okay? It's not just a string update.
We treat this as a migration, okay? Not just as a toggle. And this is really really important. When you change a model, you need to
fine-tune and then change your system prompt. You need to adapt the description of the tool calls. Why? Because every model, even if it's from the same family,
have unique characteristics. And in order to achieve and for the very least maintain the quality, if not even improve, that's what we aim for,
we have to evaluate. Okay, so we have our own evaluation system, which I can talk about later. So, we ran our all We We're running all
of our evaluations. We see today what's working well, what doesn't with the new model. Then we make the adaptations, and only after we get to the conviction that
really upgrading from Sonat 4.5 to 4.6, we actually get dramatic improvement. So, I think this is one of an an interesting takeaway. Um and as we think about it not only as a
toggle, but actually as a migration, think about when you deploy a new version to production, right? Like you don't immediately deploy to all of your
customers unless you you go YOLO. Um and therefore same thing with models. Uh by the way, it's quite funny to see how these things behave. I can tell you when
we've allowed our customers to actually choose the model on their own. So for example, not only we started with GPT but then we added a cloud family and
Gemini. We also got some interesting feedback from the other side of the spectrum where people actually told us, "Hey we're on this and I have no idea what
you've done with Ollie but I feel that now he understands me." I was like, "Wow, okay that that >> [laughter] >> that's interesting. I don't know what we've done that made
you feel this way but I will check." And when we later checked the the sessions of this specific customer we realized that all they've done is that they just
changed the model from GPT to Claude and that completely changed their experience. Same system prompt, same tools, same agent. Different model got different behavior.
So it could be bad, it could be good. But that's where we as the team developing maintaining monitoring these agents, this is where our
responsibility actually to evaluate. Um so the entire process we go through today with every new model. Right? We just got now Sonnet 5.0. We we
got new models from GPT. I can tell you we haven't yet released it to our customers. Why? Because it takes us time. It's not just
a one-day task. On average it's about 2 weeks just to evaluate these things and to make sure one we run evaluations, we then fine-tune system prompt, tool
calls, our entire agent actually to make sure it does gain improvement. Um then we release in canary. So we want to see how are you the users'
experience actually is being affected for good for bad. Um and we constantly monitor the behavior of our users of the experience they get with Ollie.
So, um that was August 2025. We learned we we now do evaluations. We don't change models that often. Um December 2025, we launched the AI. It was amazing.
We opened the the doors to all of our customers. We started to get some amazing feedbacks. Um people were amazed by the capabilities they that were shown in in
actually available through Ollie. And then something else else came up. Um users starts complaining that Ollie is consuming a lot of tokens. Now, when I heard this the first time, I
was skeptical. I was like, "What are they crying about? You know, like how do they have any idea if this is many tokens or this is small amount of
tokens? It's our agent that they they don't actually how it works." Um and honestly behind the scenes processing logs and metrics and production telemetry
does come with a lot of data, right? So, it was it didn't come to us as a surprise that it could have it could be
that this is a lot of um data or a lot of tokens. >> [snorts] >> But um one of our research engineers actually um decided to investigate this
further. And by the way, you can see all the quotes here um are anonymized, but you can see people are complaining like, "What happened with 40 million tokens?
Uh why this investigation took so long?" So, when our one of our research engineers investigated it, um he did notice something very very interesting.
Our when we look on the distribution of the tokens, so you have input tokens, output tokens, but there is another type of tokens. Anyone knows which one?
The context. Okay, I'm talking about like there's input, output. If you'll open cloud pricing or so on. Cached. Okay, exactly. Cached tokens. Do you know how much cached tokens are more
are cheaper than than regular input tokens? Usually it's about 10 times. Correct. So, 10 times is a lot of money. Okay? Uh and what we realized is that when we
looked not on how many tokens in general, but actually the distribution of token types, input, cache write, cache read, output tokens, that's when things started to click
to click, sorry. And that's when we realized that for some reason a lot of tokens are not being cached. Um and I think it's interesting because
that's something that has changed over the last year or two years with the abstraction and frameworks that we've got. So, two years ago, when you built
an agent, you would actually implement the agent loop on your own. The call to the LLM, the uh managing the tool calls and the responses and so on.
Um but with the with the evolvement of the space and with more and more SDK and agentic SDK, whether it's OpenAI agent SDK or Anthropic Claude's agent SDK and
so on, um you have this abstraction. And when you have the abstraction, you have no idea what's happening behind the scenes. And on one hand, it's great
because it allows us to develop much faster, right? But on the other hand, it makes us sometimes make mistakes we don't even realize. And that's what
happened here. So, only after investigation we realized that behind the scenes, the way our agent SDK actually manages and utilizes the system prompt and tool calls and
everything we've defined was far off from being cost-effective. So, we improved this and we got significant improvement. Uh I'm talking about give or take six, seven times more cash
tokens. So, back to our clients, I think, you know, on one hand there was a question of why do they complain about many tokens?
I think this also alleviates the question of how much value they perceive they're getting from an the agent, right? This is also another question. Uh
but on the other way around, they were actually right. Our agent was not utilizing cash as good as it should. Uh and in general, as a
benchmark, if you have less than 80% of cash tokens, um usually it means that a lot of tokens are that caching is not working properly. So, I would urge
you to actually go in and investigate that. Uh for that, obviously, you need to have history of all the conversations from production, um full tracing of what
happened behind the scenes, so you can actually debug and do these evaluations. So um we're in GA, Ollie is now quite cost-effective when comes to tokens,
using cash, and so on. Uh but then something else happened. Um customers complained that Ollie is slow. And listen, it could be, okay? It takes
time to investigate production issues, right? Like, how long would it take for a human being to do that? Sometimes it could be 15 minutes, but often times it
could be 2 hours or 5 hours, just opening logs, filtering, writing queries, uh understanding what's going on. These things take time. Um so, we decided to check that.
And we benchmark cloud code connected to our MCP, so it actually has access to all the telemetry data from production, and we compare this
with Ollie. And guess what? Ollie was not slower. It was actually faster. It took us less time. And the quality was better. So, then there is an interesting
question of why customers complain time and time again that Ollie is slow if practically, when you're looking on the numbers, the numbers tell a
different story. And hopefully you can kind of get the feeling of what's happening on the screen behind me. On this side you have the the old user
experience of Ollie. So, you see it does have streaming support. It does tell you what it is doing. But unlike cloud, look on cloud. Cloud
is constantly doing something. Maybe just writing random keywords. Herding. What is herding? Right? Then it probably will change it to something else, but there's
constantly things going on on the screen. Okay? So, it's clear that something is going on. Uh whereas in Ollie, it's less the case. And that's where where we realized,
"Hey, listen. Um actually there could be maybe maybe just maybe um Ollie is not really slower, but it just feels slower. It's about feeling, not about numbers.
Because the numbers tell us tell a different story. So, we changed that. We make Ollie think out loud. Reasoning, thinking, tool calling. Everything became
everything became verbose. Everything became clear and onto the screen. Um what we're seeing now is how Ollie actually sh- what Ollie um is doing in
terms of user experience in the new way. And what you will see is again I think in the traditional web application space we had spinners, we
had skeleton loaders, right we have all these techniques and tools to actually provide the users with the feeling that something is going on. Don't worry,
we're on it. A process is going on. Um and as you can see right now Ollie is constantly putting something on the screen. Constantly something is going
on. So it's not hidden anymore. You don't see like assessing service activity on your screen for 3 3 minutes without understanding what's going on.
So um that's another learning. Um we had 0 millisecond faster agent that felt dramatically faster. Like I I'm telling you we haven't got any complaints since then about Ollie
being slow. Um actually you know something funny the feeling we got now from customers is actually sometimes the exact opposite. Sometimes they tell us that they feel
that Ollie is too fast and they feel that it's not thinking enough. Okay, so it's really I think an interesting kind of balance >> [snorts]
>> of how do we find this balance of creating this experience of you can really on one hand don't worry the agent is working for you
on the other hand it's really doing a work you can trust. Right because the concern with Ollie being too fast is not that someone is
mad at getting fast results. They just question of whether they can trust it. So um today we're with over 1,000 production environments that are deployed monitored
constantly being investigated with Ollie whether it's scheduled tasks that are being automated, reports that are created. Um So, obviously production issues that are being investigated, um cloud cost
optimization use cases like how much am I paying for these resources? How how do these resources are actually affecting my production? Um product analytics Who is using
our features? How do they use it and so on. And just to iterate on the three learnings we had here. Uh and and by the
way, I think you know, it's it's new for everyone agents, right? And the space is changing rapidly. Like a year ago, MCP wasn't a thing yet.
Today, it's already old the old news, right? Like CLI is the new cool kid in town. So, you constantly we constantly I think learn as a community.
Uh and I think sharing what works and most importantly what didn't work and what did you learn, I think it's super important. Um so, just
to summarize three of our learnings, obviously there is a lot more. Um One, changing a model when there there's a new model that gets released or when you
want to upgrade the version of an existing model, don't treat it as a simple string replacement. Treat it seriously as a new feature. You need to thoroughly test,
evaluate, deploy safely, and monitor. Um number two, it's really fun to track activity like how many user sessions we have, how many tokens were consumed. It's great, but
it's not enough. Monitoring cache hit ratio essentially allows you to track the effect the effectiveness or the cost efficiency of your agent. Uh and lastly,
UX matters. Not only in the traditional web application world, but moreover actually in the in the new agentic world. And And as we see more users using the agentic
interface, and I think that's another something else that's interesting. We see not only developers using cloud these days, right? Like you can see marketing teams
and finance team. Like everyone is now using these tools. Um So UX matters a lot and we need to rethink these patterns and things that we used
to be um we used to do in the past. Um so hopefully it was interesting. Um I'll be more than happy to chat over our
booth if you have any questions, learnings, things you would like to share. Uh thank you very much. >> [applause] [applause] >> I think we have a few minutes for
questions. Okay. >> Thank you for this amazing presentation. Uh we have a question for you. Once you change a model, how do you know what
needs to be updated? >> It's a really really good question. Um So first and foremost, the most important thing is to have evaluation system in place. What that What does
that mean? That means we have a system with pre-made test cases and and kind of sandbox environments of production-like use real use cases. Uh and for each eval we have actually
I let let me actually explain because I think eval is a is an interesting topic. Um evals is not unit testing. And this is important. It doesn't like a test
pass or fails. Right? So we have two ways to score our agent when it comes to eval. One, did it actually achieve the the end goal? So for example, if
there's production issue and the end goal is to find the root cause, this is the success criteria. But still, think about it. Even if the
agent didn't find the root cause, it still may have been may provided some valuable insights, right? So we want also to score it positively or
negatively based on some insight and behaviors throughout the process. So, that uh lands us at a place where by the end of running all of our evils, we
have a total pass rate. So, how many of the use cases it actually got the the holy grail and actually another score. With these two, we can actually score
and tell have we improved or not or have we actually gone backwards. So, once we have these results in place, honestly, it's a lot of trial and error
and the specific developer working on the task kind of get the feeling of how this model behaves, what do I need to change in the system prompt, what do
I need to change in the tool calling. So, it's really a lot of currently at least it's a lot of gut feeling. >> How do you ensure or test that updating
all it to a new model will make it better or and not worse? Do you only check this in production through the canary release or do you have test for
your prompts? >> No, so obviously not only in production. We We are constantly testing before production and this is the evil system I was talking about. And we are constantly
by the way adding more and more evaluation test cases. So, we want to see that all the increases in score and also success rate is increasing over
time. >> And >> And we won't release it to production unless we we meet these goals. >> Yeah. How do you migrate safely from one model
to another? Do you have to rewrite the whole prompt? >> Sorry, say it again. >> How to migrate from one model to another? Do you have to rewrite the
whole prompt? >> It's a good question. Usually it's not rewriting the whole prompt. I will say that with when you move from one family, so for example
from cloud to GPT or to Gemini, yes, it is recommended to change a lot of things in the system prompt. So, it's almost a different prompt. So, we have
like a separate prompt system prompts for every model family. >> I see. Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you. >> [applause]
